title: The Human Edge: Why Brownfield Codebases Need Mob Programming, Not Just AI Vibes
gist: Two senior developers at SpareBank 1 Utvikling — which serves ~1.2m Norwegian banking customers and ~100m daily API requests — ran a deliberate 'Claude first' experiment from January to May 2026 and then reversed it, returning to hand-written TDD while keeping the LLM for analysis, telemetry and kickstarting work. Their case against AI code generation is specific to brownfield systems with 50-60 years of backend history where tacit context cannot be written down, and they argue token pricing is still subsidised to the point where a human developer may soon be cheaper than a model.

insights.claim: SpareBank 1 Utvikling deliberately went Claude-first for everything from January to May 2026 and then concluded in May to revert to traditional TDD coding, demoting the LLM to a 'super consultant' role used selectively.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: A rare documented enterprise reversal after a full-commitment trial — the kind of datapoint that rarely surfaces in vendor case studies and matters for AI coding-tool retention assumptions.
insights.quote: in May, we made a conclusion that we want to go back to a little bit more of traditional coding with TDD and use Claude more as super consultants to help us with things here and there
insights.locator: The Brownfield Challenge: Why AI Struggles with Context

insights.claim: The dominant felt cost of agentic coding for a team accustomed to shipping several times an hour was waiting — 10 to 15 minutes per Claude planning cycle — which destroyed the fast-feedback loop that drove their delivery model.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: Latency, not accuracy, is the adoption blocker for high-frequency-deploy teams; agent products competing on capability may be losing on turnaround time.
insights.quote: And suddenly we're waiting 10 to 15 minutes on Claude planning things and making things. And we were just reading, reading, reading code.
insights.locator: The Brownfield Challenge: Why AI Struggles with Context

insights.claim: The team experienced AI fatigue alongside genuine awe at the tool's power, describing the period as boring and depressing despite recognising the capability.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: Developer sentiment can decouple from tool capability; engagement metrics on AI coding tools may mask an experience problem that shows up later as churn.
insights.quote: We got a little bit bored and we got a little bit depressed at the same times that we saw that it was extremely powerful.
insights.locator: The Brownfield Challenge: Why AI Struggles with Context

themes.theme: Brownfield Context Is the Binding Constraint

insights.claim: The backend systems this team integrates with carry 50 to 60 years of history, and the accumulated quirks constitute tacit knowledge that cannot be written down for an agent.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: Context engineering has a hard ceiling in legacy-heavy sectors like banking; AI coding TAM in those verticals is structurally smaller than in greenfield software.
insights.quote: the backend systems that we integrate with have maybe 50, 60 years of history
insights.locator: The Brownfield Challenge: Why AI Struggles with Context

insights.claim: A controlled test — asking Claude to build a new REST integration by copying a very similar existing one — took roughly 45 minutes to an hour, passed human review, was shipped, and failed in production because the target API had quirks the agent could not know about.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: Demonstrates that human review of agent output does not catch context failures; the failure mode is invisible in the diff, which undercuts review-based safety arguments.
insights.quote: No, actually it didn't work because again, it didn't have the context. We would probably make the same mistake because the API had some quirks that Claude couldn't know about.
insights.locator: The Brownfield Challenge: Why AI Struggles with Context

insights.claim: Agent-generated code that looks correct on the surface can still be unfit for purpose because the backend rules it must satisfy do not make sense — surface plausibility is not a proxy for correctness in cruft-heavy systems.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: Explains why AI code review agents will underperform in legacy estates: both the writer and the reviewer lack the same missing context.
insights.quote: So even if you get code that on the surface makes sense, it's just not fit for purpose because the backend system maybe has some weird rules that just doesn't make sense.
insights.locator: AI as a Bicycle: Kickstarting Implementation vs. Generating Code

insights.claim: Letting an agent write into the domain layer reduced the team's ownership of the problem and induced complacency — approving code they did not understand — which occasionally shipped incorrect behaviour.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: Names a mechanism — comprehension debt leading to rubber-stamp review — that erodes the quality gate organisations assume they still have.
insights.quote: it reduced our ownership of the problem and it made us feel a bit complacent, I guess. We just got a bunch of code and it's like, yes, I think it looks good. I don't quite understand it.
insights.locator: The Brownfield Challenge: Why AI Struggles with Context

insights.claim: The team's initial boundary — humans own the domain layer, agents own integrations — collapsed because integrations with other systems turned out to be part of the domain, so partial delegation reproduced the same control problems.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: Clean human/agent split lines are harder to draw than they appear; 'let AI do the boring plumbing' is a weaker containment strategy than it sounds.
insights.quote: But then after a while we saw that this integration with the other systems with Claude, it's part of the domain as well because if you don't have to control of that into the domain, you get into the same problems.
insights.locator: AI as a Bicycle: Kickstarting Implementation vs. Generating Code

insights.claim: The highest-value LLM use for this team is interrogating running production systems — asking the agent how the JVM is configured, what latency looks like, and generating Grafana dashboards or ASCII graphs from telemetry.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: Observability querying, not code generation, may be the stickiest agent use case in operations-heavy orgs — relevant to where observability vendors should place agent bets.
insights.quote: ask Claude or your coding agent to talk to your application. Ask it how it's performing and in production. If you're using Java, then ask it how is the JVM configured in production?
insights.locator: The Brownfield Challenge: Why AI Struggles with Context

insights.claim: AI made the team materially more autonomous by removing dependencies on specialist teams for dashboards and pipeline scripting — and inter-team dependency, not typing speed, was their biggest source of delay.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: The real productivity mechanism is dependency elimination rather than code output — a different measurement target than lines or PRs, and a threat to internal specialist-team headcount.
insights.quote: we see that the thing that slows us down the most is when we are dependent on other people or other teams. And Claude has made us be a little bit more autonomous there on some parts.
insights.locator: The Brownfield Challenge: Why AI Struggles with Context

insights.claim: The team uses Claude to analyse and summarise a complex API's test coverage and design far faster than a human could, then implements the changes themselves — treating the agent as a kickstarter that unlocks a stalled backlog.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: 'Analyse but do not implement' is an underrated operating mode that captures most of the value with none of the comprehension debt.
insights.quote: But instead of going forward and asking to create a plan and implement everything, we will do the implementation ourselves, but it'll kickstart us.
insights.locator: The Brownfield Challenge: Why AI Struggles with Context

insights.claim: A neighbouring team built a skill that continuously monitors the codebase, writes the minimum code to turn a failing test green, and then proposes a refactoring — an attempt to fold agents into TDD rather than around it.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: Test-driven agent loops are the most promising integration pattern for teams unwilling to give up validated artifacts — a design worth watching in agent tooling.
insights.quote: every time Claude sees that there is a failing test, Claude writes the minimum amount of code needed to get the test to green. And then afterwards comes with a suggestion on how to refactor it to improve the code base
insights.locator: Team Level Experiments and Crosspolination

insights.claim: Substantial time savings come from deciding what not to build — identifying API fields no longer in use so they can be dropped — work that requires talking to other people and that an LLM will instead resolve by generating everything.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: Agents have a systematic bias toward addition, which quietly inflates the maintenance surface — a hidden long-run cost of AI-accelerated modernisation programmes.
insights.quote: an LLM will just, let me just generate everything for you so you don't have to think
insights.locator: AI as a Bicycle: Kickstarting Implementation vs. Generating Code

insights.claim: With agents able to produce large volumes of code, tests become more important, not less, because manual review or manual testing of AI output makes the human the bottleneck either way.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: Automated validation capacity is the real constraint on agent throughput — test infrastructure is the complementary investment that determines whether AI spend converts to output.
insights.quote: So you just replace the fun part of the job with a lot of boring work, which is reviewing code you haven't written or testing stuff that you haven't...
insights.locator: Team Level Experiments and Crosspolination

insights.claim: A well-factored codebase produces materially better LLM output because models excel at recognising and reproducing patterns — meaning existing code quality compounds into future AI leverage.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: Codebase quality is now a capital asset that determines the return on AI tooling — firms with clean code get more from the same model spend than those without.
insights.quote: an LLM works a lot better on a well-factored code base than on a bad code base because an LLM is really good at looking at patterns and reproducing them
insights.locator: AI as a Bicycle: Kickstarting Implementation vs. Generating Code

insights.claim: When the team asked the agent why it produced a poor construct, the answer was that it had copied an existing integration — demonstrating that agents propagate and amplify pre-existing defects.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: Agents act as defect amplifiers in legacy codebases; the cost of an unaddressed bad pattern rises with agent adoption.
insights.quote: Because you did it in the other integration that I copied
insights.locator: AI as a Bicycle: Kickstarting Implementation vs. Generating Code

insights.claim: The team frames the design question as 'code that is easy to change' rather than good versus bad code, which makes high cohesion, low coupling and TDD natural consequences rather than imposed rules.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: A reusable mental model that also happens to be the property that determines how well agents perform on a codebase.
insights.quote: Rather than debating 'good vs. bad code', focus on 'code that is easy to change'.
insights.locator: Key Takeaways

themes.theme: Mob Programming as the Human Moat

insights.claim: The team pairs or mobs on absolutely every task including PowerPoints, log inspection and analysis, rotating driver and navigator every 15 minutes in pairs and every 5 minutes in a mob of four to prevent attention loss.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: The specific rotation cadence is the operational detail that makes the practice work; teams that adopt pairing without it report the focus loss described here.
insights.quote: Everything from creating a PowerPoint, to looking at logs, to doing analysis, to everything.
insights.locator: From Pair Programming to Pair Working: Cross-Functional Collaboration

insights.claim: SINTEF researchers ran seven experiments over roughly four years at the company and published in the Journal of Systems and Software, finding that a low-commitment trial — two sessions a week for three weeks — is an effective way to introduce a new way of working.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: A peer-reviewed, cheap change-management protocol — two sessions a week — that transfers directly to rolling out any new practice, including AI tooling.
insights.quote: It's letting the team testing by just committing to trying pair programming a few times a week, let's say two sessions a week.
insights.locator: From Pair Programming to Pair Working: Cross-Functional Collaboration

insights.claim: Constant mob programming lets visiting developers from other teams reach production on their first morning — every job-shadowing visitor over the past year had code running in production before lunch on day one.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that onboarding cost is a practice problem, not a tooling problem — with direct implications for team mobility and hiring economics.
insights.quote: for the last year, we had several different developers coming, visiting us for a week and all of them had code running in production before lunch the first day
insights.locator: Building Stronger Teams: Onboarding and Psychological Safety

insights.claim: Mob programming solves the widely discussed 'junior problem' created by agentic coding, because new developers learn the domain by working inside the task rather than by having to prove themselves on an assigned ticket.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: Offers a low-cost organisational answer to the junior-pipeline collapse thesis that dominates AI labour-market commentary.
insights.quote: I think we have solved this junior problem in our team. The gap everyone is talking about when you come out of a university and start working and suddenly are using agentic coding like Claude, and you don't get to learn how to program as we did when we started working.
insights.locator: Building Stronger Teams: Onboarding and Psychological Safety

insights.claim: A strict no-outside-pull-requests policy forces external contributors into active pair programming rather than asynchronous integration, preserving team ownership and system coherence.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: An inversion of open-source-style contribution norms that becomes more defensible as agent-generated PR volume rises.
insights.quote: A strict ‘no outside pull requests’ policy forces genuine collaboration.
insights.locator: Key Takeaways

insights.claim: The arrival of Claude in January made it harder for a new developer to learn the domain, because the team spent its time reading agent output instead of the high-flow TDD and pairing loop that previously transmitted knowledge.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: Direct observed evidence that agentic workflows degrade knowledge transfer — the same risk Roblox flags but here measured on a real new hire.
insights.quote: he said it was really difficult to learn the domain because we are just asking Claude and we have to read all this stuff all the time from Claude
insights.locator: AI as a Bicycle: Kickstarting Implementation vs. Generating Code

themes.theme: Token Economics and the Bubble Call

insights.claim: Token pricing still appears subsidised, and because model progress increasingly comes from reasoning — the model prompting itself and consuming more tokens — the true cost of outsourcing coding to an LLM is not yet visible in current prices.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: The core bear case on AI coding economics: unit costs rise with reasoning depth while prices are held down, so margins or prices must move.
insights.quote: it still looks like the cost of token is subsidized. And it seems also that a lot of the progress with the models now is due to reasoning, i.e. the model prompts itself and then uses more tokens.
insights.locator: AI as a Bicycle: Kickstarting Implementation vs. Generating Code

insights.claim: Frontier model pricing is approaching the point where a human developer may simply be cheaper than the model for a given unit of work, citing Opus as expensive and a newer model priced at roughly double Opus.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: A crossover-price argument that, if it holds, caps enterprise AI coding spend regardless of capability — the metric to watch is cost per completed task versus loaded developer cost.
insights.quote: Opus is really expensive, and Fable, which was available for five minutes, was double as expensive as Opus.
insights.locator: AI as a Bicycle: Kickstarting Implementation vs. Generating Code

insights.claim: The speakers explicitly call the current environment an AI bubble and advise waiting to see whether it deflates before restructuring engineering around agents.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: Practitioner-level bubble skepticism from a team that actually ran the full experiment carries more weight than commentator skepticism.
insights.quote: I think we're still very much in a AI bubble so that I think we need to keep calm and carry on and see if the bubble deflates
insights.locator: AI as a Bicycle: Kickstarting Implementation vs. Generating Code

insights.claim: The claim that coding is solved is rejected outright, on the grounds that performance is entirely context-dependent and no developer job is at near-term risk.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: A direct counter to the labour-displacement narrative from practitioners at a systemically important bank — relevant to how quickly enterprise headcount assumptions should change.
insights.quote: I think the term that coding is solved is absolutely wrong. As I said, it's very dependent on context and what you're working with.
insights.locator: AI as a Bicycle: Kickstarting Implementation vs. Generating Code

insights.claim: The 'robots build cars in a room humans cannot enter' model for fully autonomous AI development fails because welding robots are deterministic and highly scripted while LLMs are non-deterministic by nature.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: The strongest structural objection to the lights-out software factory analogy that underpins many autonomous-SDLC pitches.
insights.quote: a robot that welds car parts, it's a highly scripted thing. It's deterministic. It does the same thing every time while an LLM, by nature, does not.
insights.locator: Building Stronger Teams: Onboarding and Psychological Safety

insights.claim: Kent Beck's 'genie' and 'slot machine' metaphors capture the LLM interaction pattern: you often get exactly what you asked for rather than what you wanted, so the failure is usually in the request, not the model.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: A durable mental model for evaluating agent failures — it relocates the improvement lever from model choice to specification quality.
insights.quote: He talks about the genie. He also called it the slot machine, which is a little bit back to the sugar rush where you put some tokens into the slot machine and then you see what comes out
insights.locator: AI as a Bicycle: Kickstarting Implementation vs. Generating Code

insights.claim: Speed without direction is worthless: an accelerator only helps if the destination and the rules are already right, which is why the team keeps humans owning domain logic.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: The compact form of their entire thesis, and the test to apply to any AI productivity claim: is the acceleration pointed at validated work?
insights.quote: You need two things to get somewhere. You need speed and direction. And if you only have speed, then obviously you're not going the right way.
insights.locator: AI as a Bicycle: Kickstarting Implementation vs. Generating Code

insights.claim: SpareBank 1 Utvikling is owned by 12 banks, serves about 1.2 million customers in a country of five million, employs around 500 people across 60 to 70 teams, and its most central account APIs handle roughly 100 million requests a day.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: Establishes that this is a systemically significant production environment, not a boutique — which is what makes the AI reversal a meaningful datapoint.
insights.quote: we have around 100 million requests every day on the most central APIs. So if we do something wrong when we are developing, we are newspaper headlines pretty fast.
insights.locator: Transcript, introductions

insights.claim: The team explicitly concedes that vibe coding and fast code generation fit greenfield startup contexts where quality is disposable and the acquirer rewrites the product anyway — the objection is context-specific, not categorical.
insights.speaker: Asgaut Mjølne Söderbom
insights.so_what: Segments the AI coding market cleanly: greenfield and disposable software is the addressable zone; regulated brownfield is not, at least yet.
insights.quote: In that case, I guess vibe coding and writing code fast would fit a lot better than it does in our system when it's a complex organization. So it really depends on the context.
insights.locator: The Brownfield Challenge: Why AI Struggles with Context
